<description>
{
 "summary": "Stops the internal HTTP server from reading and executing queued requests on a connection once a closing reply has been queued or the client is marked for disconnect. In addition, ensures that requests with conflicting framing headers (both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding) elicit a \"Connection: close\" response and terminate the connection, conforming to RFC 9112 sections 6.1 and 9.6.",
 "problem": "Following the replacement of libevent in #35182, the HTTP server continues to parse and execute requests sitting in its receive buffer after sending a response that terminates the connection. When combined with failing to close connections after receiving conflicting framing headers, an attacker or client sending pipelined HTTP commands can execute unauthorized or unintended RPC methods that should have been discarded.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"RFC 9112 section 9.6 says it must not. This is a regression from #35182, which replaced libevent: libevent's evhttp_send_done() frees the connection once a closing reply is sent, so buffered requests were never parsed.\"",
  "Commit cdd831035d and functional test in interface_http.py: demonstrates that a `setnetworkactive false` request pipelined behind a request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers executed instead of being dropped upon connection close."
 ],

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
